Hi Anna —

Thanks for laying out the exact example; super helpful. Below is a concise explanation plus a worked example you can drop into the SOW. I copied Ben and Karthik for any commercial/discount follow-ups.

Short answers (high-level)
- System messages: counted as input tokens. Any text you send as part of the request (system, user, and explicit tool inputs passed to the model) is charged as input.
- Tool calls: billing depends on how the tool is executed and how its output is consumed:
  - If a tool is executed inside the Redwood runtime and its textual output is inserted back into the model’s response (i.e., becomes part of what the model returns), those tokens are charged as output tokens.
  - If a tool call sends data to an external service and that external text is not proxied back into the model response by Redwood, then you are only charged for tokens sent to the model (input).
- Streaming: billing is based on the final, committed token counts for the request/response pair. Intermediate streamed chunks do not create additional billing events, but the final token count used for billing is the total tokens generated.
- Rounding/granularity: Redwood bills at one-token granularity (we round up to the nearest whole token). There are no 8-token buckets in the hosted rate card.

Worked example (your numbers)
- Request composition (charged as input):
  - system instruction: 40 tokens
  - user prompt: 120 tokens
  => total input tokens = 160

- Response composition (charged as output):
  - model-generated assistant tokens: 620 tokens
  - tool-returned text that is embedded in assistant response: 200 tokens
  => total output tokens = 820

- How the tool is treated: because the tool output is embedded in the assistant response, those 200 tokens are charged as output (not as additional input). If instead the tool ran externally and you did not include its text back into the model response, the 200 would not be billed as output.

- Rounding: input 160 => billed 160 (we round up to whole tokens). output 820 => billed 820. Final per-request billing is based on input and output tallies above.

Notes on discounts and committed pricing
- Per-token rounding rules do not change under committed or discounted rates; the arithmetic is the same. What changes is the per-token unit price (your negotiated rate).
- For volume commitments we can provide a blended per-1k rate for input and output or a single blended rate — Ben can propose standard bands.

I attached a tiny calculator to make it easy for procurement to plug numbers in. Let Ben know the target monthly committed spend and he’ll model a few bands.

Best,
Laura

Anna —

Adding some commercial color and a concrete price example you can paste into procurement. Assume the following (example only):
- Hosted list rate: $0.015 per 1k input tokens, $0.075 per 1k output tokens.
- You sign a 12-month commitment with a 30% discount on both input and output unit prices.

Using Laura’s billed token counts (input 160, output 820):
- List price: 
  - Input cost = 160 tokens * ($0.015 / 1000) = $0.0024
  - Output cost = 820 tokens * ($0.075 / 1000) = $0.0615
  - Per-request total (list) ≈ $0.0639

- With 30% committed discount: 
  - Input unit price = $0.0105 per 1k => input cost = 160 * (0.0105 / 1000) = $0.00168
  - Output unit price = $0.0525 per 1k => output cost = 820 * (0.0525 / 1000) = $0.04305
  - Per-request total (committed) ≈ $0.04473

If you prefer a blended single per-1k token rate for quoting in the SOW, we can create that; typically teams request either (a) separate input/output lines or (b) blended for simplicity. Important proc note: rounding is applied to token counts before multiplying by unit price (we don’t round the $ value — we calculate precisely on billed token integers).

Happy to run this across your expected monthly volume — if you share an estimate of average prompts per user session and daily sessions we’ll model monthly spend and recommended commit tier.

Cheers,
Ben
